The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle, and let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. Choose a radius $\epsilon>0$ whose closed disk subbundle $D_\epsilon\nu(K)$ is contained in $\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $S^3\setminus S$ has two components. The connected set $K$ is disjoint from $S$, so it lies in one component. The connected neighborhood $N(K)$ is also disjoint from $S$ and contains $K$, hence it lies in that same component.
The closure of the other component is a smooth three-ball disjoint from $N(K)$, so it is contained in $E_K$ and has boundary $S$. This proves irreducibility of the chosen exterior.

derivations.claim: Since $v$ is primitive, Bezout's identity gives $w\in H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ with $\det(v,w)=1$. The linear torus diffeomorphism taking the basis $(v,w)$ to the standard basis takes both curves to curves of class $(1,0)$. It is enough to prove the claim for that class.

Put the two curves in transverse position. If they intersect, lift them to the annular cover $A=\mathbb R^2/\langle(1,0)\rangle$. Each lift is an essential embedded circle, and the deck translates of each one are disjoint. In the universal cover of $A$, a lift of either circle is a proper line invariant under horizontal unit translation and contained in a bounded horizontal strip; all such lines have the same two ends. The signed intersection sum in a fundamental period is zero because both curves have class $(1,0)$. Thus intersections have both signs. Two successive intersections of opposite sign cut off a bounded region between subarcs of the two lines. Choose among such regions one with the least number of interior intersections and, among those, least horizontal width modulo deck translation. If a lifted arc entered the region, its first entry and exit would cut off a region with fewer interior intersections; if a nontrivial deck translate met it, the overlap would yield a region of smaller horizontal width. Hence its interior is disjoint from all lifted arcs and translates, and its projection is an embedded bigon in $T$. Isotoping one arc across the bigon removes two intersections and creates none. Compactness and transversality give finitely many intersections, so finitely many such isotopies make the curves disjoint.

The disjoint curves still have primitive class $(1,0)$, so neither bounds a disk. Cutting the torus along the second curve gives a connected orientable surface with two boundary circles and Euler characteristic zero, hence an annulus. The first curve remains essential in that annulus. Cutting the annulus along it gives two annuli, so it is parallel to the second curve and isotopic to it. Composing this isotopy with the finite bigon-removal isotopies in step 1.2 proves the assertion for the original pair; undoing the linear diffeomorphism proves it for $v$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1	o S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $
u_K\cong S^1	imes\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega	o S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq
u_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1	imes D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1	imes D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K	o S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. A class is primitive if it is not $m$ times another class for any integer $|m|>1$. Then $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\mu]$. The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)	o H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Let $T=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ be oriented by $dx\wedge dy$, and identify $H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^2$ in the standard basis, so the algebraic intersection of classes $v,w$ is $\det(v,w)$. Let $\gamma_0,\gamma_1\subset T$ be smooth embedded circles that are not null-homotopic. Orient them so that their homology classes agree, and suppose their common class $v\in H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ is primitive, meaning it is not an integer multiple $m u$ with $|m|>1$. Then $\gamma_0$ and $\gamma_1$ are isotopic through embedded circles in $T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in $S^3$, its Seifert genus is zero if and only if $K$ is ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms to the standard unknot.

derivations.claim: Under the full-AC hypothesis [F1], the supplier in [F2] applies. Since $c$ is essential on the torus, it is nonseparating: a separating simple curve on a genus-one surface cuts off a disk on one side and is null-homotopic. Cutting the torus along $c$ therefore gives a connected orientable surface with two boundary circles and Euler characteristic zero, hence an annulus. An embedded arc joining its two boundary circles closes after regluing to a loop meeting $c$ transversely once. The algebraic intersection is therefore $\pm1$, so $[c]$ is primitive in $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Because $c=\partial D$, its image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is zero. By [F2], write $[c]=q[\lambda]$ for an integer $q$. Since both $[c]$ and $[\lambda]$ are primitive, $q=\pm1$. Orient $c$ to make $[c]=[\lambda]$. By [F3], $c$ is isotopic on $T_K$ to a chosen simple representative of the preferred longitude.

In product coordinates $N(K)\cong S^1\times D^2$, the curve $c$ has core degree one by [F2], so its torus class is $(1,k)$ for an integer $k$. The graph $\gamma_k(t)=(e^{it},e^{ikt})$ has that class. By [F3], choose a smooth isotopy $c_s(t)=(u_s(t),z_s(t))$ on the boundary torus from $c$ to $\gamma_k$, stationary near its final time after smooth reparametrization. This isotopy need not trace an embedded annulus on the torus itself. Instead choose a smooth strictly decreasing radius $r(s)$ from $1$ to $1/2$ with nonzero derivative, and use $(s,t)\mapsto(u_s(t),r(s)z_s(t))$ in the tube. Distinct $s$ have distinct radii, while each fixed-$s$ curve is embedded; moreover the time derivative has nonzero radial component and is independent of its circle tangent. This gives a smooth embedded annulus with outer boundary exactly $c$ and inner boundary the radius-$1/2$ copy of $\gamma_k$. Continue it inward by $(r,t)\mapsto(e^{it},r e^{ikt})$ for $0\le r\le1/2$. The stationary final curve makes the collars agree; the inward annulus is smooth and regular even at $r=0$ and has core boundary $K$. The resulting annulus lies otherwise in the interior of $N(K)$.

The proper disk $D$ on the exterior side and this annulus on the tube side meet only along $c$. Their union is an embedded disk with boundary $K$; smoothing the corner along $c$ in a product collar leaves that boundary fixed. Thus $K$ bounds a smooth disk, which is a genus-zero Seifert surface. Full AC supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F4], so [F4] makes $K$ ambient isotopic to the unknot, contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore no such disk $D$ exists.

Let $D$ be a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram in an oriented $3$-sphere, with finite crossing set $C(D)$. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, define its sign as the sign of $\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$, where the two nonzero projected tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. Let $n_+$ and $n_-$ be the numbers of positive and negative crossings.

Set $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, with $\deg(1)=1$ and $\deg(X)=-1$. Its unit, multiplication, counit, and comultiplication are
$$
\eta(1)=1,\qquad m(1\otimes1)=1,\quad m(1\otimes X)=m(X\otimes1)=X,\quad m(X\otimes X)=0,
$$
$$
\epsilon(1)=0,\quad\epsilon(X)=1,\qquad \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\quad\Delta(X)=X\otimes X.
$$
Thus $m$ and $\Delta$ have quantum degree $-1$, while $\eta$ and $\epsilon$ have degree $+1$.

Choose a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on $C(D)$. A resolution state is a function $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$; at $v(c)=0$ use the A-smoothing and at $v(c)=1$ use the B-smoothing from the Kauffman source chart. Write $|v|=\sum_c v(c)$, let $D_v$ be the crossingless resolution, and let $k(v)$ be its number of circles. Assign the state module $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$. For an edge $v\to v+e_j$ changing crossing $c_j$ from $0$ to $1$, use $m$ if the local smoothing merges two circles and $\Delta$ if it splits one circle, tensored with the identity on all other factors, and multiply this map by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$. The resulting direct sum has cohomological degree
$$i(v)=|v|-n_-$$
and the generator with circle labels $1$ or $X$ has quantum degree
$$j(v)=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum_{\text{circle labels }a}\deg(a).$$
This defines the normalized integral Khovanov cube and its candidate degree-zero cochain differential; the assertion that the differential squares to zero is a separate lemma.

The Frobenius identity that controls a merge-split face is represented by the two equal composites below. The diagram records the maps only; the proof verifies the equality on the basis $\{1,X\}^{\otimes2}$ and does not rely on the drawing.

```tikzcd
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"m"] \arrow[d,"\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}"'] & \mathcal A \arrow[d,"\Delta"] \\
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}\otimes m"'] & \mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A
```

**Input:** a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ and a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on its crossing set. A diagram object is supplied as mathematical input; this procedure does not parse a serialized string.

**Output:** the normalized bigraded Khovanov cochain module $C^{i,j}(D)$ and its candidate differential $d:C^{i,j}(D)\to C^{i+1,j}(D)$, constructed by the following finite instructions.

1. Enumerate every state $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$ once. Form the crossingless resolution by using the A-smoothing at $v(c)=0$ and the B-smoothing at $v(c)=1$.
2. For each state, create one tensor factor of the integral Frobenius algebra for each resolution circle and place the resulting tensor product in cohomological degree $|v|-n_-$ and quantum degree $|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum\deg(a)$ for its circle labels $a$.
3. For each state and each crossing $c_j$ with $v(c_j)=0$, create the edge to $v+e_j$. Apply multiplication if that smoothing change merges two circles, comultiplication if it splits one circle, the identity on other tensor factors, and the sign $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$. Sum the edge maps out of every state to obtain $d$.
4. Return the finite direct sum of the state modules with these degrees and maps. The square-zero property is the separate local lemma named by `justified_by`.

Let $(D,p)$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a knot with a basepoint $p$ away from the crossings, and let $C(D)$ be its normalized integral Khovanov cochain complex. At each resolution state, let $X_p$ act by multiplication by $X$ on the tensor factor for the circle containing $p$, and by the identity on every other circle factor. The basepoint action is the direct sum of these statewise maps. Define the reduced cochain complex by
$$\widetilde C(D,p):=C(D)/\operatorname{im}(X_p),$$
with the same cohomological grading and with reduced quantum degree $\widetilde j=j-1$ for the class represented by a state whose basepoint circle is labelled $1$. Its cohomology is the reduced integral Khovanov cohomology $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$. The unknot is normalized so that its reduced group lies in bidegree $(0,0)$.

Equivalently, cut the based knot at $p$ to a one-interval tangle. Put $M=\mathbb Z$ in quantum degree $0$ with $X\cdot1=0$. A resolution with $k$ closed circles and the distinguished interval is assigned $\mathcal A^{\otimes k}\otimes M$. An edge that merges a circle into the interval uses $m_M(1\otimes1)=1$ and $m_M(X\otimes1)=0$; an edge that splits the interval uses $\Delta_M(1)=X\otimes1$, where the circle factor is written first and the interval factor second. Edges not meeting the interval use $m$ or $\Delta$. This based tangle cube is the quotient complex above, with the stated quantum shift.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram, order its crossings as $c_1<\cdots<c_n$, and form the direct sum of state modules $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$ over all functions $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$. Here $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, each crossing is changed from its A-smoothing at $0$ to its B-smoothing at $1$, and the edge map is the multiplication $m$ for a merge or comultiplication $\Delta$ for a split, multiplied by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$ on the edge at $c_j$. Then the sum $d$ of all edge maps satisfies $d^2=0$.

derivations.claim: The crossingless diagram has one based circle, hence its reduced state module is $M=\mathbb Z\{1\}$ in degree $0$ by [F2]–[F3]. There are no crossings and therefore no differential, so its cohomology is $\mathbb Z$ in degree $0$.

In the two-strand closure, the $A$-smoothing is the identity tangle and the $B$-smoothing is the cap-cup tangle. With zero, one, two, or three cap-cup smoothings, the closure has respectively two, one, two, or three circles: composing cap-cups creates one additional internal circle each time after the first. Thus the four normalized cochain degrees $-3,-2,-1,0$ have modules $M\otimes\mathcal A$, $M^3$, $(M\otimes\mathcal A)^3$, and $M\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A$, of ranks $2,3,6,4$.

The kernel of the first map gives $H^{-3}\cong\mathbb Z$. The diagonal kernel of the second map equals the image of the first, so $H^{-2}=0$. In the kernel of the last map, the $X$-coefficient triples are exactly the image of the middle map, leaving one free diagonal $1$-coefficient; hence $H^{-1}\cong\mathbb Z$. The final cokernel is generated freely by $1\otimes1$, so $H^0\cong\mathbb Z$. These computations give total rank three and include all four state degrees.

citations.quote: Fix the orientation-reversing involution $r:S^3\to S^3$ given by reflection across a fixed equatorial two-sphere containing a chosen standard unknot $U$. For a smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, its mirror is $\overline K:=r(K)$, with the orientation transported by $r$. A diagram of the mirror can be obtained by keeping the projected shadow fixed and interchanging the over- and under-crossing data at every crossing; equivalently, one may reflect the planar shadow while retaining the crossing data. These are alternative mirror conventions, not operations to perform together. Since $r^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $r(U)=U$, mirroring twice returns $K$, and $K$ is the unknot exactly when $\overline K$ is.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot and let $(D,p)$ and $(D',p')$ be finite regular oriented diagrams of $K$ with basepoints away from all crossings. Then the reduced integral groups $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$ and $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D',p')$ are isomorphic for every $(i,\widetilde j)$. In particular, they are invariant under Reidemeister moves supported away from the basepoint and under transport of the basepoint along the knot.

Assume full AC. Let $D$ be a finite based diagram of a smooth knot $K\subset S^3$ with ordered crossings $c_1<\cdots<c_n$. The singular instanton resolution complex admits a finite filtration whose first page, with its first differential, is isomorphic to the reduced Khovanov cube of the reflected based diagram $\overline D$. Its spectral sequence converges to $I^\natural(K;\mathbb Z)$. The cube sign at the edge changing $c_j$ is $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v_i}$, and the edge operation is multiplication for a merge or comultiplication for a split. Thus its $E_2$ page is the reduced integral Khovanov cohomology of $\overline D$. The claim includes coherent instanton orientations and the unlink group and saddle-map identifications; it asserts no diagram-invariance of intermediate pages.

derivations.claim: Apply [A1] to $D$. This gives a finite spectral sequence from the reduced Khovanov cohomology of the reflected based diagram $\overline D$ to the singular instanton group of $K$, with no assertion about invariance of the intervening pages.

The fixed reflection sends $D$ to a diagram of $\overline K$ and carries its marked point with it. By [F2], the reduced groups do not depend on the chosen based diagram of $\overline K$. Thus the $E_2$ page from step 1.1 is the stated knot invariant $\widetilde{Kh}(\overline K;\mathbb Z)$, with its bigrading forgotten.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot and let $(D,p)$ and $(D',p')$ be finite regular oriented diagrams of $K$ with basepoints away from all crossings. Then the reduced integral groups $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$ and $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D',p')$ are isomorphic for every $(i,\widetilde j)$. In particular, they are invariant under Reidemeister moves supported away from the basepoint and under transport of the basepoint along the knot.

derivations.claim: Suppose $\widetilde{Kh}(K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ as a total graded group. Set $J=\overline K$. By [F1], $\overline J=K$. The $E_2$ group in [A1] for $J$ is therefore $\mathbb Z$, so its rationalization has dimension one.

Put $S=\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$. Localization $S^{-1}(-)=(-)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ preserves exact sequences: if $f:A\to B$ is injective and $f(a)/s=0$, some $t\in S$ has $f(ta)=0$, hence $ta=0$ and $a/s=0$; if $g:B\to C$ follows $f$ and $g(b)/s=0$, choose $t\in S$ with $tb\in\ker g=\operatorname{im}f$, say $f(a)=tb$, so $b/s=f(a)/(ts)$; if $g$ is surjective, each $c/s$ is the image of a lift divided by $s$. Thus localization commutes with kernels, images, and homology.

The spectral sequence in [A1] is obtained by taking successive homology pages of a finite filtered complex. Exact localization therefore identifies its rationalized pages with the pages of the rationalized filtered complex, and identifies the localized abutment with $I^\natural(\overline K;\mathbb Q)$. The $E_2$ page has rational dimension one by step 1.1.

On each finite-dimensional rational page, the next page is homology. For any differential $d$ on a finite-dimensional vector space $V$, rank-nullity gives $\dim H(V,d)=\dim V-2\dim\operatorname{im}d\le\dim V$. Iterating this inequality over the finite spectral sequence bounds the total dimension of $E_\infty$ by its one-dimensional $E_2$ page; since the finite abutment filtration has associated graded $E_\infty$, its total dimension equals $\dim_{\mathbb Q} I^\natural(\overline K;\mathbb Q)\le1$.

By [A2], this target has dimension at least one, so it has dimension one. The rank-detection clause of [A2] implies that $\overline K$ is the unknot; applying the same reflection gives that $K$ is the unknot.

Conversely, for the crossingless one-circle unknot diagram the reduced complex has the single generator from [F2] and no differential. Its total cohomology is therefore $\mathbb Z$ in bidegree $(0,0)$. This proves the converse and hence the stated equivalence.

finite_checks.claim: The crossingless one-circle quotient has a single Z generator in bidegree (0,0).
A one-dimensional E2 page gives total E-infinity dimension at most one; finite convergence identifies this with abutment dimension.

boundaries.reason: The theorem is about a smooth knot, which is nonempty by definition.
